summary: A browser-based cooperative mission simulator for ages 7–12 that teaches real-world space engineering trade-offs and communication delays using authentic NASA space weather and lunar data
details:
NASA ARASAKA — Project Details

What the project does and how it works

NASA ARASAKA is a two-player, real-time space-mission simulation. Two users connect over the network and cooperate to keep a spacecraft and its crew alive during a series of space-weather emergencies.

The system follows a client–server architecture. A central Python server (server.py) holds the single source of truth — the state of the spacecraft (Spaceship) and its four crew members. Two PyQt5 desktop clients connect to this server over TCP and exchange newline-delimited JSON messages:

• Mission Control — a ground-station operator who sees ship telemetry (oxygen, energy, hull integrity, cabin temperature, module statuses), loads emergency scenarios, issues mission orders, and approves or rejects crew proposals.

• Onboard Commander — the crew representative aboard the ship, who sees the same telemetry plus private crew health data (individual health and heart rate), executes orders, sends proposals back to Mission Control, and chats with the ground.

Each scenario is based on a real category of space weather. When Mission Control loads a scenario, the server applies initial damage to ship systems and crew, sends an alert to both clients, and presents three response options. The chosen option applies delta changes to ship parameters and — critically — to crew health and heart rate through a dedicated apply_crew_delta pathway. The server then checks game-over conditions (oxygen depletion, energy depletion, hull destruction, temperature extremes, or total crew incapacitation), broadcasts the outcome, and synchronizes both clients.

The design deliberately enforces information asymmetry: Mission Control cannot see crew health, and the Onboard Commander cannot issue scenario decisions. Only by communicating — through chat, orders, and proposals — can the two players complete the mission. This mirrors real mission operations, where ground control and flight crew each hold half the picture.

Benefits

• Educational value. Every scenario is grounded in real NASA space-weather categories (Radiation Belt Enhancement, Solar Flare, Solar Energetic Particles, Coronal Mass Ejection) drawn from the NASA DONKI database. Players learn how space weather affects spacecraft systems and human health without needing a physics background.

• Teamwork and communication. The asymmetric information model forces genuine collaboration — neither player can win alone. This makes the game useful for training communication under pressure, a skill relevant well beyond aerospace.

• Low barrier to entry. No installation beyond Python and PyQt5. The server is pure standard library. Two laptops on the same Wi-Fi can play in minutes.

• Extensibility. Scenarios are plain Python dictionaries. Adding a new emergency, a new module, or a new crew member requires editing a single file (server.py or game/ship.py) — no architectural changes.

• Accessibility for demonstration. Mission Control includes an offline simulation mode, so the project can be demonstrated even without a running server — useful for hackathon judging or classroom settings.

Intended impact

The project aims to make space-weather literacy tangible. Space weather is an abstract, invisible threat that most people never think about, yet it directly affects satellites, astronauts, aviation, and power grids. By turning real DONKI event categories into playable decisions with immediate consequences, NASA ARASAKA helps players feel why radiation shielding matters, why backup antennas exist, and why mission rules exist around solar particle events.

A secondary impact is pedagogical: the project is a complete, working example of client–server multiplayer design with role-based state, real-time synchronization, and turn-based scenario resolution — a template that students or educators can fork for their own simulations.

How the project is creative

Creativity shows up in three places.

First, the information-asymmetry mechanic. Most cooperative games give both players the same view and simply require coordination. NASA ARASAKA splits the picture: Mission Control sees the ship but not the people; the Commander sees the people but not the whole ship. This forces conversation rather than parallel action — a design choice borrowed from real mission operations but rarely used in small educational games.

Second, the use of real scientific categories as game content. Instead of inventing fictional aliens or warp drives, the project treats actual DONKI event classes as scenario seeds. Each scenario carries a NASA reference link and a "what is real vs. what is simulated" note, so players learn something verifiable. This is a more honest form of educational game design than fictionalizing the science.

Third, the crew-health model. Rather than treating the crew as a single health bar, every crew member has individual health and heart rate, and both respond dynamically to ship conditions — low oxygen raises heart rate, hull breaches hurt, life-support failure compounds damage. This turns the crew from a number into a system that reacts to the ship, which makes scenario consequences feel personal.

Factors considered by the team

• Scientific honesty. We explicitly distinguish real data (DONKI event categories, event IDs, Shackleton Crater) from simulated values (damage, injuries, outcomes). The README and in-game dialogs both carry this disclaimer, so judges and players are never misled.

• Fairness of difficulty. Each scenario offers three responses: a recommended option with trade-offs, a mediocre option, and a clearly bad option. The recommended option is not free — it still costs energy or crew health — so players must weigh consequences rather than pick a "correct answer."

• Network reliability. The server uses per-client send locks and a global state lock, so concurrent scenario loads and order executions cannot corrupt the shared Spaceship state. Clients poll on a 50 ms timer and buffer partial messages, so slow networks do not lose data.

• Role exclusivity. One active client per role: if a second client joins with the same role, the older connection is cleanly dropped. This prevents state ambiguity during demos.

• Demonstrability. Mission Control ships with an offline simulation mode, so the project can be shown without a live server — a safeguard for hackathon conditions.

• Portability. No cloud dependencies, no database setup, no web stack. Two laptops with Python and PyQt5 can play in under five minutes, which matters for a live judging session.

• Accessibility of code. Scenario data, ship state, and event handlers live in separate files (SCENARIOS in server.py, Spaceship in game/ship.py, events in game/events.py), so future contributors can extend one layer without touching the others.
